This is not a list of the top ten words that changed my life. It is a list of the words that I consider to be essential. There are no objects. No “table,” “water,” or “road.”
I love these words, and I am going to do my best to live by them.
Hello: I remember the first time that someone introduced me as “my friend.” It was such a large word at the time. Now I try to use the word whenever I can. I hope that when they hear it, they feel as I did when I was first called by that name.
Help/Danger: An action of love is ambiguous. Cooking, driving across town, and remembering birthdays can all leave doubt. But a hand on a shoulder can say “I’m sorry.”
Believe/Trust: I have been given this gift many times in my life. Some have been quiet, “I believe in you.” Somewhere else, someone has held me up longer than any act of rescue. In all cases, they have spoken volumes.

Since then, researchers have reported in Obstetrics & Gynecology that the rate appeared to roughly double within a few years around 2011.
The task force brings together physicians, nurses, epidemiologists, and public health experts to review individual maternal deaths case by case. The group has found that Black women in Texas die from pregnancy-related causes at far higher rates than white or Hispanic women.
The panel has also highlighted the role of substance abuse in maternal death. The task force’s early analysis found that Black women accounted for about one in nine births in Texas but nearly three in ten maternal deaths.
Its extension is on the special session agenda.
As it is, Texas Medicaid covers about half of the state’s births — but often, only for the period of pregnancy. After that, pregnancy-related Medicaid for many low-income mothers ends roughly 60 days after delivery.
Some mothers lose access to treatment in those weeks when they need it most. It’s a problem that Texas lawmakers need to fix.
In the meantime, though, Texas lawmakers can take another step toward preventing these needless deaths by extending the task force’s life.
The Legislature created the Texas Maternal Mortality and Morbidity Task Force in 2013. The panel’s mission is to reduce maternal deaths in Texas through better data and research. The task force was scheduled to expire this year unless lawmakers acted.

We tend to use gross domestic product (GDP) as a measure of well-being. There is, however, a major limitation of this approach.
- GDP measures economic output. It is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period of time. It does not, however, measure human welfare or well-being.
- GDP measures economic output, not human welfare. It measures what is produced, not how it is produced. It does not reflect income distribution. It also does not consider the quality of the environment.
- GDP does not reflect income distribution. If the top 1 percent of households in a country earns half of all income, then GDP per capita may look healthy, but the typical household may struggle.
- GDP does not reflect the quality of the environment. A factory that pollutes a river adds to GDP through its output, but the lost water quality and health costs of pollution are not subtracted.
- In a country where the top 1 percent of households earns half of all income, GDP per capita may look healthy, but the typical household may struggle.

A common claim is that 7% of communication is words, 38% tone and 55% body language. The figures come from Albert Mehrabian’s studies in the late 1960’s. He measured how people judged feelings and attitudes when someone’s words clashed with their tone or expression. He did not measure the overall proportions of communication.
But when Mehrabian himself later wrote a book on body language he stated clearly that his research “cannot be used to gauge the relative importance of verbal and nonverbal messages.” In other words, body language is important, but the figures are not a good measure of that importance.
But even if body language is not as important as the oft-quoted numbers suggest, it is still important. So what does body language say about you? What does your body language say to others?
The most important thing to know is that your body language should always be consistent with your words. If you are delivering a lecture on tax law, people are not going to be watching your hands for clues to what you are saying. But when you are communicating with another person and you want them to trust what you are saying, your body language needs to be consistent with your words.
The most important thing to remember is to be consistent with what you say. If you say one thing and your body language tells another story, you will confuse your audience. Your audience will not trust you.
When you talk, your audience is watching your body language. If your words say one thing but your body language says another, your audience will look at your body language for guidance. If you want to be taken seriously, you need to ensure that your body language is consistent with your words. You want to be trusted, right?
A sincere apology delivered while you are scrolling your phone lands as an insult. The most important thing to remember is to be consistent. When you are talking to someone you need to talk to them.
When you apologise, don’t say you are sorry while you are distracted by something else. If you are sincere about your apology, make sure you are looking at the person to whom you are apologising.
When you ask someone a question, make sure you are looking at them while they answer. They will know you are not really interested if you are not looking at them.
When you are talking to someone, make sure your body language is consistent with what you are saying.
There are many different aspects of body language and you may well be communicating with your body in ways that you are not even aware of. The most important thing is to be consistent with what you are saying and what you are showing.

Business tort law refers to the legal process that addresses wrongs done by one business to another. It can also refer to the liability of businesses for wrongs done to consumers and bystanders.
Business tort law is a broad area of law. It can involve a wide range of potential claims, such as:
- Defamation
- Fraud
- In invasion of privacy
- Consumer protection violations
- Unintentional acts, such as negligence
- Intentional acts, such as acts of violence
- Products liability
A business can be held liable for a tort even without a contract. A delivery driver who causes a crash, a website that publishes a false accusation, or a manufacturer whose product injures a bystander can all face liability without any contract in place.
In the United States, Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act generally shields online platforms from liability for content posted by their users. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enforces laws against unfair or deceptive practices and provides free resources for consumers and companies.

Seaweed is sold as dried snacks, powdered “sea greens,” kelp tablets, and capsules promising thyroid support, detox, or metabolic balance. Many people take seaweed as a concentrated source of iodine, hoping to improve thyroid function. But is this a good idea? In this post, I’ll look at the potential benefits and harms of seaweed consumption.
First, a few facts about seaweed:
What is seaweed, anyway? Microalgae include organisms like Chlorella and Arthrospira (spirulina), while macroalgae include kelp, nori, and wakame. In Japan, seaweed is eaten as part of meals, in varied types and amounts. For instance, nori and wakame contain much less iodine than kombu. However, microalgae, including Chlorella and Arthrospira (spirulina), are sometimes promoted as food or dietary supplements. Some strains of microalgae are above 50 percent protein by dry weight. Spirulina is often promoted as a vitamin B12 source, but much of its B12 is a form that humans can’t use.
Why do people take seaweed? Japanese iodine intake swings from day to day, and is not a steady, high, supplement-like dose. In Japan, iodine intake comes mostly from seaweed, and Japanese people have some of the highest iodine intakes in the world. Many estimates put Japan’s average daily iodine intake at one to several milligrams per day, well above Western upper limits. Iodine-related hypothyroidism has been documented in Japan, particularly among heavy consumers of kombu.
Do the Japanese tolerate high iodine intake? Iodine intake in Japan may be high, but there’s a big difference between Japan’s tradition of eating seaweed as part of meals, in varied types and amounts, and the use of concentrated seaweed supplements. Japan’s tradition doesn’t show that a concentrated kelp capsule is harmless for an adult raised on a low-iodine diet. Japanese clinicians often advise patients with certain thyroid conditions to limit seaweed.
In Japan, iodine intake swings from day to day and is not a steady, high, supplement-like dose. There may be a tolerance for such a wide range of iodine intake, but it’s possible that there’s a tradeoff, where the risk of iodine-related hypothyroidism goes up with a high intake.
Iodine needs
How much iodine do we need? Adults need about 150 µg iodine per day, and pregnancy requires about 220 µg iodine per day. Breastfeeding requires about 290 µg iodine per day.
